c.tagline: The birthplace of alpinism, beneath Western Europe's highest peak and the world's highest cable car ascent
langs: English (widely spoken due to international mountaineering tourism)

card: Widely accepted; cash useful for mountain refuges and small shops

taxi.fare: Metered, roughly €4 flag fall plus per-km rate
taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; the free local bus (Chamonix Bus) covers most valley trips

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number; mountain rescue (PGHM) is reached via 112

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: Central Chamonix is compact and walkable; the surrounding villages (Argentière, Les Praz, Les Bossons) require the free local bus or a car

safety.safety: Very safe town; the main risks are mountain-related (weather, altitude, glacier travel) rather than crime
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare; standard mountain safety precautions apply for hikers and climbers

hood_landmark.Chamonix Centre: The Aiguille du Midi cable car base station
hood_landmark.Argentière: The Grands Montets ski lift base
hood_landmark.Les Praz-de-Chamonix: The Flégère cable car base and golf course
hood_landmark.Le Tour: Le Tour's quiet ski lift base at the valley's northern end

avoid.reason: Crime is minimal; the real risks are mountain hazards, plus occasional ski/gear theft outside bars and rental shops.

hood_desc: The lively pedestrian core with the Aiguille du Midi lift, most restaurants, shops, and mountaineering outfitters; the natural base for any visit.
A quieter alpine village further up the valley, home to the Grands Montets ski area and a more local feel.
A residential hamlet with its own cable car up to the Flégère balcony trail, good for a calmer stay with valley views.
A small settlement near the Bossons glacier, one of the most easily viewed glaciers in the valley from the road.
The northernmost, quietest village in the valley, popular with families and cross-country skiers seeking fewer crowds.

water.note: Alpine tap water is excellent and safe to drink.

transit.sys: Chamonix Bus (free local network) and the Mont-Blanc Express mountain train linking valley villages
transit.pay: Free on Chamonix Bus with a valid lift pass or lodging card; the Mont-Blanc Express requires a ticket
transit.note: The free valley bus makes a car unnecessary for most visitors

transport.air: Geneva Airport (GVA, Switzerland), about 1 hr away; Lyon-Saint Exupéry (LYS) is a further alternative
transport.train: Mont-Blanc Express narrow-gauge train connects Chamonix to Martigny, Switzerland; TGV to Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet connects to Paris
transport.bus: Direct shuttle buses run from Geneva Airport
transport.car: Well connected via the Mont Blanc Tunnel to Italy and the A40 motorway from Geneva/Lyon

airport.name: Geneva Airport
airport.transport: Direct shuttle bus, train via Martigny, or rental car

net.m: Strong 4G/5G in the valley, patchier at altitude
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.ap: An Orange, SFR, or Bouygues tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.r: Service is included by law; rounding up is a nice gesture, not expected

places.name: La Cabane des Praz

landmarks: Aiguille du Midi
A vertiginous cable car rockets from town to 3,842 meters, where terraces, the 'Step into the Void' glass box, and Mont Blanc fill the horizon.
Mer de Glace and the Montenvers Railway
A century-old red cog train climbs to France's largest glacier, where an ice grotto carved anew each year glows blue inside the frozen sea.
Mont Blanc
Western Europe's highest summit at 4,806 meters dominates every Chamonix vista, a dazzling white dome that has defined alpinism since its first ascent in 1786.
Le Brévent Cable Car
Rising on the valley's sunny side to 2,525 meters, Brévent's platforms serve the classic full-frontal panorama of the entire Mont Blanc massif.
Lac Blanc
This jewel-like alpine tarn in the Aiguilles Rouges reserve mirrors the Mont Blanc range perfectly, reached by a beloved hike from the Flégère lift.
Balmat and Saussure Monument
In the pedestrian heart of town, the bronze of pioneers Jacques Balmat and Horace-Bénédict de Saussure points forever toward the summit they conquered.
Glacier des Bossons
Tumbling almost into the valley floor, this dramatic icefall descends farther than any other Alpine glacier, viewable from an easy chairlift and forest trails.
La Flégère
A sun-drenched balcony lift station on the Grand Balcon Sud trail, prized for effortless hikes with nonstop views across to glaciers and granite spires.
Musée Alpin
Housed in a Belle Époque palace hotel, Chamonix's alpine museum traces crystal hunters, pioneering mountaineers, and the 1924 first Winter Olympics.
Vallée Blanche Panoramic Gondola
From the Aiguille du Midi, tiny red bubbles glide five kilometers over the glacier-draped Vallée Blanche toward Italy's Pointe Helbronner, an unforgettable high-alpine crossing.

train.note: Chamonix sits on the narrow-gauge Mont-Blanc Express, which runs the length of the valley from Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet through Chamonix and Vallorcine to Martigny in Switzerland, where you can join the Swiss network for Geneva, Lausanne, Zermatt and the Simplon route to Italy. The French section is run by SNCF and the Swiss section by TMR, and the two halves have separate fares, so buy the Swiss leg from TMR or SBB. There is no direct TGV to Chamonix itself - high-speed trains from Paris and Lyon terminate at Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet, where you change onto the valley train, adding about 45 minutes. Winter timetables are denser than summer ones, but engineering closures with replacement buses are common in the shoulder seasons.

bus.note: Coaches use the Chamonix Sud bus station, a five-minute walk from the centre, and the SNCF station forecourt. The Italian service runs through the Mont Blanc tunnel and reaches Courmayeur in about 45 minutes, Aosta in around 1h30m and continues to Turin and Milan; note that SAT merged with Borini in September 2025, so timetables now appear under the Borini name and tickets for the Geneva line are sold as FlixBus. Geneva, 80 km away, is the main gateway and is served both by scheduled coaches and by a dense network of door-to-door shared shuttles that must be booked ahead in ski season. Carry a passport - the tunnel and the Swiss border are both crossed on these routes.

ferry.note: Chamonix lies in an Alpine valley at 1,035 m with no navigable water, so there are no ferries of any kind. The nearest passenger boats are the CGN paddle steamers on Lake Geneva, about 90 minutes away, and the Lake Annecy cruise boats roughly two hours away.

half.name: Courmayeur
half.blurb: Italian resort town on the far side of the Mont Blanc massif, reached through the road tunnel.

half.name: Martigny
half.blurb: Swiss valley town with well-preserved Roman ruins, an amphitheater, and the Fondation Gianadda art and archaeology museum.

half.name: Annecy
half.blurb: Alpine lake town of canals and a medieval old town, often called the Venice of the Alps.

half.name: Geneva
half.blurb: Lakeside Swiss city with the towering Jet d'Eau fountain, a historic old town and international organizations along Lake Geneva.
